newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Rerating hopes boost Hong Kong stock flows.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Rerating hopes boost Hong Kong stock flows.

text.p: A burst of liquidity into the Hong Kong stock market has breathed new life into the territory's shares, with hopes of a market re-rating propelling the Hang Seng index to a record close.

Hong Kong stocks have traded traditionally at lower multiples than their regional counterparts, but solid earnings and a variety of China growth plays have investors calling for a higher price/earnings (PE) ratio than the current multiple of about 13 times 1997 earnings.
"What people are asking themselves right now is is Hong Kong going to be re-rated," said Abhijit Chakrabortti, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers.
"Hong Kong gives you an average of about 13 percent EPS (earnings per share growth) but the market is up 22 percent so it has given you way beyond earnings growth," he said.
SOUTHEAST ASIA FUNDS BOOST HONG KONG STOCK MARKET LIQUIDITY

Analysts said a flow of funds from other Southeast Asian markets has boosted liquidity in the Hong Kong stock market. So far this month, the daily average turnover is HK$7.10 billion (US$973 million) compared with HK$5.08 billion in September.
The Hang Seng index scored a record close last Wednesday at 12,250.57 points and ended on Friday at 12,218.40, down 24.07 points on the day but up 312.89 on the week.

"It is quite evident that international funds are rebalancing in favour of Hong Kong much to the detriment of Thailand and the Philippines and maybe even Singapore," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas.

Pauline Gately, regional strategist at Merrill Lynch, agreed: "I do think we are seeing some switching in the region and it would seem to be that they are crystallising some of those profits in the Philippines," she said.
"In Thailand, some of the stale bulls that have been sitting on long positions in the market are selling."
HONG KONG'S PEG TO U.S DOLLAR HELPS ATTRACT INVESTORS
In its fourth quarter market outlook "Liquidity-driven rally", Tai Fook Securities said the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar would also help attract overseas investors.
"With the pegged exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar to the U.S. dollar, there is definitely limited exchange risk for U.S. investors," it said.
Chakrabortti said European investors could also find reasons to invest in Hong Kong, particularly with slow growth among Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries.

"The real interest they would of course have would stem from the fact that Hong Kong right now is being seen as something of a stable growth environment at a time of decelerating growth in Asia and at a time of fairly tentative or fairly weak OECD recovery," he said.
While Hong Kong trades at a multiple of about 13.5 times 1997 earnings, Malaysia is trading at about 19 times, Singapore 20 or 21 times and South Korea about 13, said Chakrabortti.
"Relatively Hong Kong's valuation is quite low. Its PE is the lowest within the regional markets," said Patrick Chia, research director at China Everbright Research.
HONG KONG COMPANIES SHOW SOLID EARNINGS GROWTH
Meanwhile, Hong Kong companies have given evidence of solid earnings growth while other markets are struggling.

"A lot of earnings revisions in Hong Kong have been positive and that has not been the case in some of the other markets where I think we are seeing deteriorating fundamentals due to cyclical factors and other reasons," said Fernow.
Chakrabortti said investors who paid higher multiples for growth in other Asian markets were disappointed.
"There have been big growth shocks in Thailand and South Korea, Singapore and even to a certain extent India," he said.

"Every time they (investors) see growth disappointment or earnings disappointment they realise they overpaid so what they have decided to do, in a very unstable growth environment, is to go for the only areas where they see strong growth momentum -- and that is why they pick Hong Kong," said Chakrabortti.
"CHINA FACTOR" ALSO ATTRACTS INVESTORS

Analysts said the "China factor" was also attracting investors to Hong Kong. "People are looking for a play on the China economy. Hong Kong is the most direct play," said Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Interest rates (in China) have come off since May and that is expected to result in future to improvements in China and I think people are looking at further interest rate cuts."
Analysts said Hong Kong firms are starting to reap the fruit of investments in China, particularly in the infrastructure sector.
"As these infrastructure projects provide stable and mostly guaranteed returns, quality of earnings are enhanced and justified with higher PE multiples for the market as a whole," said Tai Fook.
Analysts said improving China-Hong Kong relations should also contribute to a re-rating. Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule on midnight June 30, 1997.

"It seems that the transitional period for Hong Kong should have no problems and I think maybe even after 1997 for the first few years under Chinese rule I think the local economy can prosper further and that will help give some valuation to the local market," said Chia.
Tai Fook said unfavourable factors have already been discounted. "Given the unfavourable factors were well-discounted, the re-rating of Hong Kong's financial markets should be impending," it said.
However, some analysts said investors were being short-sighted in thinking Hong Kong should be re-rated.
"I think there is some scope for PE revaluation but it is relatively limited in the short-term, one year view," said Alan Hutcheson, director of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I think you need a longer term time frame to remove the discount," he said.

Chakrabortti said investors were discounting too little earnings growth in Sotuh Korea and Malaysia and too much in Hong Kong. He said South Korea should produce 16 percent earnings growth in 1997 from a 40 percent fall in 1996 and Malaysia 16 percent growth on average between 1996 and 1997.

"If you believe that Hong Kong over five years will grow at 12 percent and Malaysia over five years will grow at 17 percent then over five years that means that...you have a greater risk element in Hong Kong," said Chakrabortti.
He said Hong Kong looked expensive. "I think the earnings stream in Hong Kong is seen more stable in the near term. But there is only so much you can pay for it."

"I would hate to see it (the Hang Seng index) beyond 12,500. The momentum is very strong; it could easily go well beyond 12,500 and we would like to see it trade more in the 11,000 to 11,500 range because that is fairer value," he said.
But Merrill's Gately said the Hang Seng index could reach 13,500 to 13,700 by the first quarter of next year "if the interest is maintained and it is reinforced by some more positive interest".
